questions.question: Explain how facilitated diffusion differs from active transport.

marking_points.criterion: Facilitated diffusion moves substances down a concentration gradient through membrane proteins.
Active transport uses energy to move substances against a concentration gradient.

questions.model_answer: Facilitated diffusion moves substances down a concentration gradient through membrane proteins. Active transport uses energy to move substances against a concentration gradient.
marking_rules: Accept scientifically equivalent wording. Award each distinct point once.
Withhold a point if directly contradicted. Do not reward unsupported claims.
Numerical method and result are separate points where listed. Equivalent consistent units are acceptable.
Provisional point-based practice rubric; not an official OCR marking or levels-of-response scheme.
questions.common_misconception: All movement through a membrane protein requires ATP.
hints: Identify the key ideas in membranes and transport. State the relevant relationship before applying it.
One starting point: Facilitated diffusion moves substances down a concentration gradient through membrane proteins.
questions.follow_up: A cell accumulates mineral ions although their concentration is already higher inside. Explain why simple diffusion cannot account for this.

repair.explanation: Facilitated diffusion can use membrane proteins without ATP. It moves substances down their concentration gradient, unlike active transport.
repair.worked_example:
A cell accumulates mineral ions although their concentration is already higher inside. Explain why simple diffusion cannot account for this.
Net simple diffusion would move ions down their concentration gradient rather than accumulate them against it. Active transport using carrier proteins and energy can account for the accumulation.
repair.check: Explain how facilitated diffusion differs from active transport.

questions.question: Explain how rough endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi apparatus contribute to secretion of a protein.

marking_points.criterion: Ribosomes on rough ER synthesise the protein, which enters the ER for transport.
Golgi modifies and packages the protein into vesicles for secretion.

questions.model_answer: Ribosomes on rough ER synthesise the protein, which enters the ER for transport. Golgi modifies and packages the protein into vesicles for secretion.
marking_rules: Accept scientifically equivalent wording. Award each distinct point once.
Withhold a point if directly contradicted. Do not reward unsupported claims.
Numerical method and result are separate points where listed. Equivalent consistent units are acceptable.
Provisional point-based practice rubric; not an official OCR marking or levels-of-response scheme.
questions.common_misconception: The Golgi apparatus makes proteins by translating the genetic code.
hints: Identify the key ideas in cell organelles. State the relevant relationship before applying it.
One starting point: Ribosomes on rough ER synthesise the protein, which enters the ER for transport.
questions.follow_up: An antibody-secreting cell has extensive rough ER and many Golgi vesicles. Link each feature to its function.

repair.explanation: Ribosomes synthesise proteins by translation. The Golgi modifies and packages proteins rather than translating the code.
repair.worked_example:
An antibody-secreting cell has extensive rough ER and many Golgi vesicles. Link each feature to its function.
Rough ER provides many attached ribosomes for producing protein antibodies. Golgi and vesicles process, package and transport antibodies for release.
repair.check: Explain how rough endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi apparatus contribute to secretion of a protein.

questions.question: Give two structural differences between a bacterial cell and a typical animal cell.

marking_points.criterion: A bacterial cell lacks a membrane-bound nucleus; an animal cell has one.
Bacteria have 70S ribosomes while the animal cell cytoplasm has 80S ribosomes.

questions.model_answer: A bacterial cell lacks a membrane-bound nucleus; an animal cell has one. Bacteria have 70S ribosomes while the animal cell cytoplasm has 80S ribosomes.
marking_rules: Accept scientifically equivalent wording. Award each distinct point once.
Withhold a point if directly contradicted. Do not reward unsupported claims.
Numerical method and result are separate points where listed. Equivalent consistent units are acceptable.

questions.common_misconception: A bacterium has no nucleus, so it has no DNA.
hints: Identify the key ideas in prokaryotes and eukaryotes. State the relevant relationship before applying it.
One starting point: A bacterial cell lacks a membrane-bound nucleus; an animal cell has one.
questions.follow_up: A micrograph shows a small cell with cytoplasm, ribosomes and DNA but no membrane-bound nucleus. Explain why it is likely prokaryotic and why it is still a cell.

repair.explanation: Bacteria contain DNA even though they lack a membrane-bound nucleus. Their main DNA is located in the cytoplasm in a nucleoid region.
repair.worked_example:
A micrograph shows a small cell with cytoplasm, ribosomes and DNA but no membrane-bound nucleus. Explain why it is likely prokaryotic and why it is still a cell.
Absence of a membrane-bound nucleus with DNA in the cytoplasm supports a prokaryotic identification. It still has a cell membrane, cytoplasm and genetic material needed for cellular processes.
repair.check: Give two structural differences between a bacterial cell and a typical animal cell.

questions.question: Contrast the cell envelopes of Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria.

marking_points.criterion: Gram-positive bacteria have a thick peptidoglycan wall and no outer membrane.
Gram-negative bacteria have a thinner peptidoglycan layer and an outer membrane.

questions.model_answer: Gram-positive bacteria have a thick peptidoglycan wall and no outer membrane. Gram-negative bacteria have a thinner peptidoglycan layer and an outer membrane.
marking_rules: Accept scientifically equivalent wording. Award each distinct point once.

questions.common_misconception: All bacteria respond identically to the same antibiotic because all have cell walls.
hints: Identify the key ideas in gram staining. State the relevant relationship before applying it.
One starting point: Gram-positive bacteria have a thick peptidoglycan wall and no outer membrane.
questions.follow_up: An antibiotic enters Gram-positive cells more readily than Gram-negative cells. Suggest an envelope-based explanation and one limitation of identifying species this way.

repair.explanation: Bacterial susceptibility differs between species and strains. Envelope permeability and resistance mechanisms can affect antibiotic entry or action.
repair.worked_example:
An antibiotic enters Gram-positive cells more readily than Gram-negative cells. Suggest an envelope-based explanation and one limitation of identifying species this way.
The Gram-negative outer membrane can restrict entry of some antibiotics. Antibiotic susceptibility varies between species and strains, so this result alone does not uniquely identify a species.

questions.common_misconception: A ten-times larger image must always resolve ten-times smaller structures.

questions.common_misconception: An electron microscope can routinely observe living cells moving in water.
hints: Identify the key ideas in tem sem and cell counts. State the relevant relationship before applying it.
One starting point: TEM can show internal ultrastructure in a thin specimen.
questions.follow_up: A technician needs to count cells and distinguish their appearance. Compare a haemocytometer with an electronic Coulter counter.

questions.common_misconception: Magnification is image size multiplied by actual size.
hints: Identify the key ideas in microscopy practical. State the relevant relationship before applying it.
One starting point: Use a thin specimen so light can pass through it.
questions.follow_up: An image measures 30 mm and the cell is actually 50 micrometres long. Calculate magnification and show the unit conversion.

repair.explanation: Magnification is image size divided by actual size. Both sizes must be expressed in the same units.

An image measures 30 mm and the cell is actually 50 micrometres long. Calculate magnification and show the unit conversion.
30 mm is 30000 micrometres. Magnification is 30000 divided by 50 = 600 times, with no unit.

questions.question: Explain why an eyepiece graticule must be calibrated using a stage micrometer.

marking_points.criterion: The graticule divisions have no fixed specimen length without calibration.
Calibration relates graticule divisions to a known length at the chosen objective magnification.

questions.model_answer: The graticule divisions have no fixed specimen length without calibration. Calibration relates graticule divisions to a known length at the chosen objective magnification.

questions.common_misconception: One graticule division always represents one micrometre at every magnification.
hints: Identify the key ideas in graticule calibration. State the relevant relationship before applying it.
One starting point: The graticule divisions have no fixed specimen length without calibration.
questions.follow_up: At one objective, 40 graticule divisions match 100 micrometres. A cell spans 12 divisions. Calculate its length and state what happens if the objective changes.

repair.explanation: Graticule divisions must be calibrated for each objective. Changing the objective changes the specimen length represented by one division.
repair.worked_example:
At one objective, 40 graticule divisions match 100 micrometres. A cell spans 12 divisions. Calculate its length and state what happens if the objective changes.
Each division represents 100 divided by 40 = 2.5 micrometres, so the cell is 30 micrometres long. The graticule must be recalibrated for the new objective.

questions.common_misconception: Soil pH is a biotic factor because plants respond to it.
hints: Identify the key ideas in distribution and energy transfer. State the relevant relationship before applying it.

questions.follow_up: A consumer receives 500 J in food and transfers 60 J into new biomass. Calculate percentage transfer efficiency and explain one reason it is below 100%.

questions.common_misconception: Aluminium sulfate has formula AlSO4 because one ion of each type is always required.

In a secondary alcohol, that carbon is attached to two other carbons.

questions.model_answer: In a primary alcohol, that carbon is attached to one other carbon, with methanol as a special case. In a secondary alcohol, that carbon is attached to two other carbons.

questions.common_misconception: A secondary alcohol contains two OH groups.
hints: Identify the key ideas in alcohols and combustion. State the relevant relationship before applying it.
One starting point: In a primary alcohol, that carbon is attached to one other carbon, with methanol as a special case.
questions.follow_up: Balance complete combustion of ethanol, C2H5OH, and state a safety consequence of incomplete combustion.

questions.question: Describe how to obtain initial reaction rate from a gas-volume versus time graph.

marking_points.criterion: Draw a tangent to the curve at the start.
Calculate its gradient as change in volume divided by change in time, with units.

questions.model_answer: Draw a tangent to the curve at the start. Calculate its gradient as change in volume divided by change in time, with units.
marking_rules: Accept scientifically equivalent wording. Award each distinct point once.
Withhold a point if directly contradicted. Do not reward unsupported claims.
Numerical method and result are separate points where listed. Equivalent consistent units are acceptable.
Provisional point-based practice rubric; not an official OCR marking or levels-of-response scheme.
questions.common_misconception: The initial rate is always the final gas volume divided by the total reaction time.
hints: Identify the key ideas in rates practical. State the relevant relationship before applying it.
One starting point: Draw a tangent to the curve at the start.
questions.follow_up: A tangent rises by 18 cm3 over 12 s. Calculate initial rate and explain why a gas leak would bias the measurement.

repair.explanation: Initial rate is the gradient at the start of the curve. Final volume divided by total time is an average over the interval, not generally the initial rate.
repair.worked_example:
A tangent rises by 18 cm3 over 12 s. Calculate initial rate and explain why a gas leak would bias the measurement.
Initial rate = 18 divided by 12 = 1.5 cm3 s-1. A leak allows some gas to escape measurement and underestimates collected volume or rate.
repair.check: Describe how to obtain initial reaction rate from a gas-volume versus time graph.

questions.common_misconception: A water temperature rise means combustion has positive delta H.
hints: Identify the key ideas in combustion calorimetry. State the relevant relationship before applying it.
One starting point: Some released energy heats the surroundings or apparatus rather than the water.
questions.follow_up: Burning 0.0100 mol fuel heats 0.100 kg water by 15.0 degrees C. Use c=4200 J kg-1 degrees C-1 to estimate molar enthalpy of combustion.

repair.explanation: Combustion transfers energy to the surroundings and has negative delta H. The water temperature rise measures energy gained by the water, not a positive reaction enthalpy.
repair.worked_example:
Burning 0.0100 mol fuel heats 0.100 kg water by 15.0 degrees C. Use c=4200 J kg-1 degrees C-1 to estimate molar enthalpy of combustion.
q = 0.100 times 4200 times 15.0 = 6300 J = 6.30 kJ. Delta H = -6.30 divided by 0.0100 = -630 kJ mol-1, assuming all heat reaches the water.
repair.check: Explain why simple flame calorimetry often underestimates the magnitude of an exothermic enthalpy of combustion.

questions.common_misconception: A watt is a unit of electrical energy rather than rate of energy transfer.

questions.follow_up: A 12 V device draws 0.50 A for 120 s. Calculate power and electrical energy transferred.

questions.common_misconception: Adding a parallel resistor always increases total resistance.

questions.common_misconception: The smaller resistor in a series potential divider always has the larger voltage across it.

questions.follow_up: A 12 V supply feeds a 4 kilohm upper resistor and a 2 kilohm lower resistor. Calculate output across the lower resistor.

hints: Identify the key ideas in acoustic impedance. State the relevant relationship before applying it.
One starting point: Acoustic impedance Z equals density times sound speed.
questions.follow_up: Two media have acoustic impedances 2.0 and 6.0 in the same units. Calculate intensity reflection coefficient using ((Z2-Z1)/(Z2+Z1)) squared.

hints: Identify the key ideas in cohorts and meta-studies. State the relevant relationship before applying it.

hints: Identify the key ideas in correlation and conclusions. State the relevant relationship before applying it.
One starting point: A third variable or bias may produce the observed association.
questions.follow_up: Ice-cream sales and sunburn cases rise together. Evaluate the claim that ice cream causes sunburn.

questions.common_misconception: Reviewing only evidence that supports your belief is a reliable way to eliminate bias.
hints: Identify the key ideas in bias in communication. State the relevant relationship before applying it.
One starting point: Confirmation bias favours information supporting existing beliefs.
questions.follow_up: A review finds only published positive trials, while several registered negative trials have no results available. Explain the concern and a response.

repair.explanation: Selecting only confirming information introduces confirmation bias. Seek relevant contradictory evidence and use transparent selection criteria.
repair.worked_example:
A review finds only published positive trials, while several registered negative trials have no results available. Explain the concern and a response.
Missing negative results may bias the apparent treatment effect through publication or reporting bias. Search trial registries, request missing results and state the limitation rather than assuming the published sample is complete.
